Chapter 7: Navigating Triggers and the Lingering Shadows of the Past.
Even when new routines start to feel comfortable and hope begins to grow again, the past has this uncanny way of sneaking back in, doesn’t it? Sometimes, it’s the smallest thing—a word, a scent, maybe just a song playing in the background—that can send memories flooding in, way more powerful than you’d expect.
Those moments can be jarring. You might suddenly feel like you’re right back in the middle of old fears and doubts. It’s like your body remembers before your mind even catches up—your heart starts pounding, your hands get clammy, and all you want to do is escape.
Healing, it turns out, isn’t a straight path. Sometimes, a single phrase overheard in a busy market can pull you right back. The world feels smaller, and it’s tough to remember how far you’ve come.
Most people don’t realize just how much energy it takes to handle these triggers. There’s always that urge to avoid anything that might stir up the past—to keep your world safer, but smaller at the same time. But over time, it becomes clear: facing those triggers, instead of running from them, is really where your power comes back.
With the gentle support of a therapist, one survivor learned a different approach. When those old feelings bubbled up, they started to pause instead of pushing them away. They’d actually name the emotion—maybe it was fear, or sadness, or even anger—and just let it sit there for a moment. Sometimes, just acknowledging the feeling was enough to break its hold. Other times, reaching out to a friend and sharing what was going on made all the difference.
Little by little, those triggers lost some of their grip. Instead of feeling weak, each moment became a sign of resilience. Every time the past resurfaced, it was a chance to practice self-compassion and remind themselves just how far they’d come. The shadows didn’t vanish completely, but they stopped shaping every part of the present.
The way you navigate triggers is deeply personal. For some, it might mean picking up a journal or turning to art. For others, it’s all about movement—taking a walk, dancing, or simply taking a few deep breaths. What matters most is being willing to stay present, to trust that the pain will eventually pass, and to celebrate every small victory along the way.
Over time, the world starts to feel less threatening. What used to be a source of shame or fear becomes proof of survival. The real journey isn’t about erasing memories; it’s about weaving them in—making peace with what’s happened, so you can truly live in the present.
